unit-alg-t2-01.title: Topic 2 · 2-1 Vertex Form of a Quadratic Function
unit-alg-t2-01.source: enVision Algebra 2 Lesson 2-1: Vertex Form of a Quadratic Function

cards.def:
**y = a(x − h)² + k, where (h, k) is the vertex of the parabola.**
• a controls how the graph opens and stretches.
• h and k slide the vertex left/right and up/down from the origin.
cards.hint: h and k name the vertex directly — that's the whole point of this form.

cards.def:
**The turning point of a parabola — its lowest point if it opens up, its highest if it opens down.**
• In vertex form y = a(x − h)² + k, the vertex is (h, k).
• Every other point on the graph is a mirror image of another point across the vertex.
cards.hint: The vertex is where the graph changes direction — rising becomes falling, or the reverse.

cards.def:
**The vertical line x = h that splits a parabola into two mirror-image halves.**
• It always passes through the vertex.
• Any point on the graph has a matching point the same distance on the other side of this line.
cards.hint: Fold the graph along this line and the two halves land on each other exactly.

cards.def:
**The U-shaped (or upside-down U) graph of any quadratic function.**
• Every parabola is a transformation of the parent function f(x) = x².
• It opens upward or downward, never sideways, for a function of x.

**The sign of a decides which way the parabola opens; the size of a decides how narrow or wide it is.**
• a > 0 opens upward, a < 0 opens downward.
• |a| > 1 stretches the graph narrower; 0 < |a| < 1 compresses it wider.

**h slides the graph left or right; k slides it up or down.**
• (x − h) shifts opposite to the sign written — (x − 3) moves the graph right 3, (x + 3) moves it left 3.
• +k moves the graph up; −k moves it down, exactly as written.
cards.hint: h is the trap: the sign inside the parentheses is the OPPOSITE of the shift direction.

cards.def:
**All real numbers, every time — (−∞, ∞).**
• A parabola stretches left and right forever, so there is no x-value it can't take.
• This is true no matter what a, h, or k are.
cards.hint: Only the range changes parabola to parabola. The domain never does.

cards.def:
**Everything from the vertex's y-value out to infinity, in the direction the parabola opens.**
• Opens upward (a > 0): range is [k, ∞).
• Opens downward (a < 0): range is (−∞, k].
cards.hint: The range always starts at k — the only question is which direction it goes.

cards.term: Writing vertex form from a vertex and a point
cards.def:
**Substitute the vertex for (h, k), then use the other point to solve for a.**
• Plug the vertex in first — h and k are done.
• Plug the known point's x and y into what's left, and solve the one remaining equation for a.
cards.hint: Only one unknown is left once the vertex is in — it's always solvable in one step.

cards.def:
**Flips a parabola upside down without moving its vertex.**
• g(x) = −f(x) reflects f over the x-axis.
• A reflected upward-opening parabola becomes downward-opening, same vertex.
cards.hint: Reflecting only changes the SIGN of a — h and k don't move.

cards.def:
**Multiplying by a number bigger than 1 makes the parabola narrower; multiplying by a fraction between 0 and 1 makes it wider.**
• g(x) = 4x² is narrower than f(x) = x².
• g(x) = 0.25x² is wider than f(x) = x².
cards.hint: Bigger |a| pulls the graph in tight. Smaller |a| lets it spread out.

cards.term: Example: reading a vertex from an equation
cards.def:
**For g(x) = 2(x − 3)² − 4, the vertex is (3, −4).**
• a = 2, so it opens upward and is stretched narrower than x².
• Axis of symmetry: x = 3. Range: [−4, ∞).
cards.hint: Read h and k straight off the equation — no computing needed in vertex form.

cards.def:
**For g(x) = −½(x + 2)² + 6, the vertex is (−2, 6) and the graph opens downward.**
• a = −½ is negative (opens down) and a fraction (wider than x²).
• Range: (−∞, 6].
cards.hint: h = −2 because (x + 2) is really (x − (−2)) — the sign flips.

cards.def:
**A launched object's height over time is a quadratic function — its vertex is the peak of the flight.**
• The vertex's x-value is the TIME of the maximum height.
• The vertex's y-value IS the maximum height.
cards.hint: In a height-vs-time graph, the vertex answers both "when" and "how high" at once.

cards.def:
**Substitute a point you know is on the graph and confirm both sides match.**
• The vertex should always check out exactly, since you built the equation from it.
• A second point (like a y-intercept) is what actually confirms you solved for a correctly.
cards.hint: The vertex checking out doesn't prove anything — you need a SECOND point to catch a mistake in a.

questions.q: In vertex form y = a(x − h)² + k, what point does (h, k) name?
opts: A point where the graph crosses the x-axis
questions.hint: It's right in the name of the form.
steps: Vertex form is built specifically to make one point easy to read.
That point is the parabola's turning point — where it changes from rising to falling, or the reverse.
(h, k) names exactly that point: the vertex.

ex.main: **The vertex.** That's the entire reason this form exists — every other form of a quadratic hides the vertex behind computation.

questions.q: What is the vertex of g(x) = 5(x − 6)² + 1?
questions.hint: Read h and k straight from the equation.
steps: Match the equation to y = a(x − h)² + k.
Here h = 6 and k = 1 — read directly, no sign flip needed since it's already (x − 6).
So the vertex is (6, 1).

ex.main: **(6, 1).** In vertex form the vertex is never computed — it's read straight off the equation.

questions.q: What is the vertex of h(x) = −3(x + 4)² − 2?
questions.hint: (x + 4) means h is negative — watch the sign flip.
steps: Rewrite (x + 4) as (x − (−4)) to match the vertex form pattern y = a(x − h)² + k.
So h = −4, not 4.
k = −2, read directly. The vertex is (−4, −2).

ex.main: **(−4, −2).** The sign inside the parentheses is the opposite of h — this is the single most common vertex-form mistake.

questions.q: For f(x) = −7(x − 2)² + 9, which way does the graph open?
opts: Downward, because a is greater than 1 in size
questions.hint: Only the SIGN of a decides the direction.
steps: a = −7 in this equation.
A negative a always opens the parabola downward, regardless of its size.
So the graph opens downward because a is negative — not because of its size, and not because of k.

ex.main: **Downward, because a is negative.** The size of a affects width, not direction — those are two separate jobs.

questions.q: Which equation is narrower than the graph of f(x) = x²?
questions.hint: Narrower means |a| is bigger than 1.
steps: A vertical stretch (narrower graph) happens when |a| > 1.
g(x) = 6x² has |a| = 6, which is greater than 1 — narrower.
g(x) = 0.3x² has |a| = 0.3, which compresses it wider instead, and the other two options don't change a at all.

ex.main: **g(x) = 6x².** Multiplying by a number bigger than 1 pulls the graph in tighter around its axis of symmetry.

questions.q: The graph of f(x) = x² is translated 5 units left and 3 units down. What is the resulting equation?
questions.hint: Left means h is negative, and the sign inside the parentheses flips.
steps: A translation left by 5 means h = −5, written as (x − (−5)) = (x + 5).
A translation down by 3 means k = −3.
Combining both: g(x) = (x + 5)² − 3.

ex.main: **g(x) = (x + 5)² − 3.** Left and down each move exactly one number, and the sign inside the parentheses flips for the left/right one.

questions.q: What is the range of g(x) = 4(x − 1)² + 8?
questions.hint: Check the sign of a first — it decides which direction the range goes.
steps: a = 4 is positive, so the parabola opens upward.
An upward-opening parabola's range starts at its vertex's y-value and goes up forever.
k = 8, so the range is [8, ∞).

ex.main: **[8, ∞).** Opens upward, so every y-value from the vertex up is reachable — but nothing below it.

questions.q: What is the range of g(x) = −2(x + 3)² + 5?
questions.hint: a is negative here — which direction does that send the range?
steps: a = −2 is negative, so the parabola opens downward.
A downward-opening parabola's range goes from negative infinity up TO its vertex's y-value.
k = 5, so the range is (−∞, 5].

ex.main: **(−∞, 5].** Opens downward, so 5 is the highest y-value the graph ever reaches.

questions.q: What is the domain of g(x) = −100(x − 50)² + 3?
questions.hint: This is true for every quadratic function, no matter the numbers.
steps: A parabola extends left and right without any restriction, no matter what a, h, or k are.
Even with large or unusual coefficients like −100 and 50, that fact doesn't change.
So the domain is all real numbers.

ex.main: **All real numbers.** The domain of a quadratic function never depends on a, h, or k — only the range does.

questions.q: A parabola has vertex (3, −2) and passes through the point (5, 6). What is its equation in vertex form?
questions.hint: Substitute the vertex, then use the point to solve for a.
steps: Substitute the vertex (3, −2) for h and k: y = a(x − 3)² − 2.
Substitute the point (5, 6): 6 = a(5 − 3)² − 2, so 6 = 4a − 2.
Solve: 8 = 4a, so a = 2. The equation is y = 2(x − 3)² − 2.

ex.main: **y = 2(x − 3)² − 2.** The vertex fills in h and k for free; the extra point is only there to pin down a.

questions.q: A parabola has vertex (−1, 4) and y-intercept 10. What is its equation in vertex form?
questions.hint: A y-intercept is the point where x = 0.
steps: Substitute the vertex (−1, 4): y = a(x + 1)² + 4.
The y-intercept is the point (0, 10), so substitute: 10 = a(0 + 1)² + 4, meaning 10 = a + 4.
Solve: a = 6. The equation is y = 6(x + 1)² + 4.

ex.main: **y = 6(x + 1)² + 4.** A y-intercept is really just a point where x happens to be 0 — same method as any other point.

questions.q: A parabola has vertex (4, −3) and passes through (6, 5). What is its equation in vertex form?
questions.hint: Same method as before, different numbers — substitute the vertex, then solve for a.
steps: Substitute the vertex (4, −3): y = a(x − 4)² − 3.
Substitute the point (6, 5): 5 = a(6 − 4)² − 3, so 5 = 4a − 3.
Solve: 8 = 4a, so a = 2. The equation is y = 2(x − 4)² − 3.

questions.q: A parabola has vertex (−2, 6) and y-intercept −6. What is its equation in vertex form?
questions.hint: The y-intercept is negative — expect a to come out negative too.
steps: Substitute the vertex (−2, 6): y = a(x + 2)² + 6.
The y-intercept is (0, −6), so substitute: −6 = a(0 + 2)² + 6, meaning −6 = 4a + 6.
Solve: −12 = 4a, so a = −3. The equation is y = −3(x + 2)² + 6.

ex.main: **y = −3(x + 2)² + 6.** A y-intercept below the vertex, with the graph opening upward from k = 6, forces a negative — the parabola has to open downward to reach it.

questions.q: A diver's board is 8 ft above the water. She jumps and reaches her highest point of 40 ft after 1 second. Using vertex form with x as time in seconds, what equation models her height?
questions.hint: The peak of the flight is the vertex. The launch point is a second point, at x = 0.
steps: The peak height of 40 ft at 1 second is the vertex: (1, 40). Substitute: y = a(x − 1)² + 40.
The board height of 8 ft is the height at x = 0: 8 = a(0 − 1)² + 40, so 8 = a + 40.
Solve: a = −32. The equation is y = −32(x − 1)² + 40.

ex.main: **y = −32(x − 1)² + 40.** a comes out negative because the height has to come back DOWN from the peak to reach 8 ft — a positive a would send it upward forever instead.

questions.q: What is the standard-form equation (y = ax² + bx + c) equivalent to y = −32(x − 1)² + 40?
questions.hint: Expand (x − 1)² first, then distribute the −32.
steps: Expand (x − 1)²: (x − 1)² = x² − 2x + 1.
Distribute −32: −32(x² − 2x + 1) = −32x² + 64x − 32.

ex.main: **y = −32x² + 64x + 8.** Expanding vertex form always gets you standard form — the vertex information is just harder to see once it's expanded.

questions.q: Martin says the graph of g(x) = (x + 6)² is the graph of f(x) = x² translated 6 units RIGHT. What is his error?
opts: (x + 6) translates the graph LEFT, not right
g(x) should be (x − 6)² to be a valid translation
The vertex of g is (0, 6), not (−6, 0)
There is no error — Martin is correct
questions.hint: Check the sign inside the parentheses against the actual direction it shifts.
steps: To match y = a(x − h)² + k, rewrite (x + 6) as (x − (−6)), so h = −6.
A negative h shifts the graph in the negative x-direction, which is LEFT.
So Martin has the direction backwards: (x + 6) shifts the graph left, not right.

ex.main: **(x + 6) translates the graph LEFT, not right.** This is the single most common vertex-form error — the sign written is the opposite of the shift direction.

questions.q: What is the axis of symmetry of g(x) = 9(x − 7)² + 2?
questions.hint: The axis of symmetry is a vertical line through the vertex.
steps: The axis of symmetry always has the form x = h.
In this equation, h = 7.
So the axis of symmetry is x = 7.

ex.main: **x = 7.** It's always a vertical line, always written x = (something), and it always matches h exactly.

questions.q: Two parabolas both have vertex (2, 5). One has a = 3, the other has a = 0.5. Which statement is true?
opts: The a = 3 graph is narrower than the a = 0.5 graph
The a = 3 graph is wider than the a = 0.5 graph
Both graphs are exactly the same width
The vertex tells you which one is wider, not a
questions.hint: Compare the SIZE of each a, not its sign.
steps: Both values of a are positive, so both parabolas open upward — the vertex alone doesn't distinguish their width.
|3| is bigger than |0.5|, and bigger |a| always means a narrower graph.
So the a = 3 graph is narrower than the a = 0.5 graph.

ex.main: **The a = 3 graph is narrower.** Width is entirely a question of |a| — the vertex has nothing to do with it.

questions.q: A kicked ball's height is modeled by y = −16(x − 0.8)² + 12.24, where x is time in seconds. A second ball is modeled by y = −16(x − 0.6)² + 9.76. Which ball reaches a greater maximum height, and how do you know?
opts: The first ball — its vertex's y-value, 12.24, is greater than 9.76
The second ball — it reaches its peak sooner, at 0.6 seconds
They reach the same height — both have a = −16
The first ball — it was in the air longer
questions.hint: Maximum height is read from the vertex, not from the time it happens.
steps: The maximum height of each ball is the y-value of its vertex, k — not how quickly it gets there.
The first ball's vertex is (0.8, 12.24), so its maximum height is 12.24.
The second ball's vertex is (0.6, 9.76), so its maximum height is 9.76. 12.24 is greater, so the first ball reaches higher.

ex.main: **The first ball, because 12.24 > 9.76.** Reaching the peak sooner says nothing about how HIGH that peak is — those are two different numbers in the vertex.

questions.q: Which of these is written in vertex form?
questions.hint: Vertex form always has a squared binomial, written as (x − h)².
steps: Vertex form has the specific shape y = a(x − h)² + k — a single squared binomial, plus a constant.
y = 3x² + 12x − 7 is standard form (expanded, no binomial squared).
y = (x − 2)(x + 6) is factored form (two separate binomials multiplied). y = 2x + 5 isn't quadratic at all. Only y = −4(x − 5)² + 9 has the vertex-form shape.

ex.main: **y = −4(x − 5)² + 9.** It's the only option with a single squared binomial plus a constant — the exact shape of vertex form.
